Notes: Year Established = -50 (c.; end of the Ptolemaic period / 1st c. BCE, midpoint convention), the earliest DATED Jewish presence at Edfu found. J. Manteuffel (Polish excavator of the Franco-Polish Tell Edfu excavations 1937-39), 'Tell Edfu' (1948): a group of ostraca shows that 'at the end of the Ptolemaic period Jews already formed a considerable part of the inhabitants of Edfu' (translated from Polish); cites O.E. 366 (Apollonios son of Dositheos paying the tax on fruit), O.E. 368 (a list incl. a 'Iosepos hiereus' [priest]) and O.E. 370 of the 1st c. BCE (list of wine merchants incl. Semitic names Abdelos, Autkis). He states Jews in the Ptolemaic period lived freely in various quarters of the town, traded and farmed. No number given; 'considerable part' is qualitative, so Population blank. Context (not rows): W. Clarysse (JJP 32, 2002) notes the Jewish name Jes(ous) was 'a common name, also in Ptolemaic Edfou' (undated within the Ptolemaic period); two Jewish travellers' graffiti (Ptolemaios son of Dionysios and Theudotos son of Dorion, 'Ioudaioi') at the Paneion of el-Kanais c. 60 km east of Edfu, dated 2nd half 2nd-1st c. BCE, are outside the town and not counted.

c. late Ptolemaic period (Manteuffel: 'fin de l'époque ptolémaïque'; midpoint convention for 1st c. BCE). Manteuffel, 'Quelques textes provenants d'Edfou', Journal of Juristic Papyrology 3 (1949): ostracon O.E. 368 'contient une liste des participants des boissons paschales' (a collection for Passover drinks) - evidence of communal Jewish religious practice at Edfu; with the wine-merchant list O.E. 371 he concludes commerce at Edfu at the end of the Ptolemaic period was largely in Jewish hands and that Jews then lived in various quarters of the town. Presence of an organized community; no count.

c. late Ptolemaic period (context dated by the author to the 2nd half of the 2nd - 2nd half of the 1st c. BCE; midpoint convention). S. Struffolino, 'Due ebrei benedicono Dio presso un tempio di Pan', Axon 4.2 (2020): discussing two Jewish travellers on the desert road to Apollinopolis Magna, states 'sappiamo però che anche qui viveva una comunità giudaica integrata' (a Jewish community lived at Apollinopolis Magna/Edfu), citing Kasher 1985, 161-7 for Jews there as village scribes and in other administrative and military functions. Presence of a community; no number.

c. early Roman period: CPJ V covers 30 BCE-117 CE (midpoint 44); individual dates not given in the source, some texts may fall after 74 CE. BMCR 2023.06.31 (review of Hacham & Ilan, CPJ V, 2022): CPJ V begins with sixteen Demotic ostraca from Edfu (entries 620-626), tax receipts of Jews bearing Greek and Hebrew names, attesting 'the impact of Egyptian language and culture on Jews in the Thebaid', plus Greek tax receipts from Edfu (627-632). The editors reconsider Tcherikover's dating (no longer nearly all Flavian) and regard the district where most Jewish ostraca were found as 'the home of many Jews' but 'not, as Tcherikover held, a Jewish quarter.' CPJ II had 249 Jewish ostraca from Edfu (a count of documents, not people). No population figure.

c. 70-71 CE. Clarysse, Remijsen & Depauw, 'Observing the Sabbath in the Roman Empire: a Case Study', Scripta Classica Israelica 29 (2010): ostracon CPJ II 240 (70-71 CE) names Aischylos son of Josephos as a tax collector of Edfu's Jewish community. The authors describe 'a small Jewish community in Edfu' whose ostraca, found in houses near the Ptolemaic temple, 'belonged to a few Jewish families' (CPJ II 160-408); they paid the ordinary capitation taxes and, after 70 CE, the Jewish tax (2 denarii = 8 dr. + 2 ob. agio + aparche = 9 dr. 2 ob.), until 117 CE when the community 'was decimated' in the Jewish revolt. 'A few Jewish families' is not a count, so Population blank.

2 June 72 CE (Payni 8, year 4 of Vespasian). Manteuffel, JJP 3 (1949): the Jewish tax ('timē dēnariōn duo Ioudaiōn', later 'Ioudaion telesma') was due from Vespasian's year 2 but first paid in year 4, as shown by O.E. 40, a receipt of Niger son of Antonius Rufus for 8 dr. 2 ob. 'Jews' two denarii' for year 2. Manteuffel also records under Vespasian the large family of Antonius Rufus with five sons, and holds that in the Roman period the Jews were confined to the walled 4th quarter of Apollinopolis (a view later rejected: see BMCR row). Tax payable by all Jews aged 3 to 60/62, incl. women, freedmen and slaves. Presence of several families; no total given.
